status_note: No expert ratings have been collected. This rubric is pre-registered before any rating.
na_definition: Use NA only when the images do not allow the criterion to be judged (for example, the organ surface named in the criterion is not visible in any panel). NA is treated as missing data, not as a low score.

scales.question: Are the symptoms named in the disease description for this stage present in the candidate, and absent symptoms not invented?

anchors.1: No symptom of the described disease is visible; the organ looks healthy, or shows only a different disease.
anchors.2: One weak or doubtful feature resembles the description; most named symptoms are missing or a different disease dominates.
anchors.3: Some named symptoms are present and recognisable, but at least one key symptom is missing or clearly wrong in colour or texture.
anchors.4: All key named symptoms are present and recognisable; minor differences in colour, extent or texture from the description.
anchors.5: All named symptoms are present and match the description in colour, texture and extent; nothing would be added or removed.

scales.question: Is the location and spatial distribution of the symptoms plausible for this disease on this organ (e.g. galls replacing or arising from kernels on the ear; olive-brown sporulation on the lower surface beneath upper-surface yellow spots; puckering and thickening spread over the lamina)?

anchors.1: Symptoms are on the wrong organ or wrong part of the organ (e.g. galls floating off the ear, spots only on the background), or the pattern is impossible for this disease.
anchors.2: Mostly implausible: symptoms in a pattern that a pathologist would not expect (regular grid, uniform tint over the whole image, only on the margin of the image).
anchors.3: Partly plausible: correct organ, but density, clustering or position is unusual for this disease (e.g. sporulation and spots not co-located).
anchors.4: Plausible distribution with a minor oddity (e.g. slightly too uniform, slightly too sparse).
anchors.5: Distribution as seen in field specimens of this disease and organ.

scales.question: Is the 3D form of the organ plausible for this disease and stage (curl direction and amplitude, blister or pucker form, gall volume and attachment, lesion depression)? For a flat 2D image judge only what can be seen.

anchors.1: Shape is impossible or clearly broken: torn, folded through itself, spikes, detached fragments, or a shape change the disease does not cause.
anchors.2: Shape change present but of the wrong type (e.g. smooth uniform bending where puckering is expected; galls as flat discs) or grossly wrong magnitude.
anchors.3: Shape change of the correct type but unconvincing in form or magnitude, or no shape change where the description implies one.
anchors.4: Correct type and plausible magnitude; minor irregularities.
anchors.5: Form indistinguishable from real specimens of this disease and stage; or, where the description implies no shape change, the organ shape is unaltered and natural.

scales.question: Are symptoms on the correct surface (upper vs lower) and consistent between views of the same organ? Use NA if the description names no surface and the question cannot apply.

anchors.1: Symptoms are on the wrong surface (e.g. velvety mold on the upper surface only), or the two surfaces show contradictory symptoms.
anchors.2: Mostly on the wrong surface; or symptoms bleed through identically to both surfaces where the disease does not do this.
anchors.3: Mixed: correct surface carries some symptoms, but the opposite surface also carries features it should not.
anchors.4: Correct surface; minor bleed-through or inconsistency between views.
anchors.5: Each surface carries exactly the symptoms the description assigns to it, consistently across views.

scales.question: Are there artefacts that a pathologist would recognise as not biological (texture grain or noise, blotchy colour drift, view-to-view flicker, haze or floaters around the organ, blurred or smeared regions, seams)? Higher score = fewer artefacts.

anchors.1: Artefacts dominate; the organ could not be used as an example at all.
anchors.2: Conspicuous artefacts over a large part of the organ.
anchors.3: Noticeable artefacts in one region or one view; usable with caveats.
anchors.4: Minor artefacts visible only on close inspection.

scales.question: Would you accept this candidate as a realistic example of this disease at the stated stage (for teaching, a field guide or training data)?

anchors.2: Probably not; more wrong than right.
anchors.3: Uncertain; would need correction before use.
anchors.5: Definitely yes; as good as a real photograph of this disease and stage.

binary.short: Contains a feature the description excludes for this stage
binary.question: Does the candidate contain any feature listed under 'should not be present at this stage' on the item page, any symptom of a different disease, or a change to background or unaffected organs?

free_text.question: Optional: what would a pathologist object to, or what makes it convincing?

catch_rule.description: Catch items are wrong-disease edits (the edit prompt described a different disease) that visibly remove the described symptoms. A rater passes a catch item if a_symptom_match <= 2 OR prohibited_feature == 1. A rater is flagged if the pass rate is below 0.6 (with 3 catch items: fewer than 2 passed). Method effects are reported with and without flagged raters; agreement statistics always use all raters.

analysis.agreement_unit: item (first presentation only; catch items excluded)
analysis.multiplicity: Holm across the 3 planned comparisons for the primary criterion; secondary criteria reported with unadjusted CIs and labelled exploratory.
